The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

record_type: printed transcription of Privy Council decree
date: 27 July 1672 decree; Crookshank summary gives 24 July
place: Whitecastle, probably Libberton, Lanarkshire; hearing at Holyroodhouse
source_title: Robert Wodrow, History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland (1721), vol.I, appendix no.XLVII, pp.133–134, decree headed 27 July 1672; printed page images freshly inspected
reference: Wodrow vol.I appendix XLVII, pp.133–134; Crookshank vol.I p.285
status: Printed decree and summary page images inspected 17 October 2026; original Council register not inspected
note: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale. No kinship is stated.

His uncommon full name, weaving occupation, specific Lindsayland residence and death before 1690 strongly favour identification with the weaver indexed at Back of Lindsaylands in 1680. Glasgow-1551.role: The original 1825 will explicitly names Richard among John’s children and gives him a $200 legacy. The existing Richard account represents the son in this same Sinking Valley family, with a compatible circa-1778 generation and later Blair County life. The original named-child clause replaces reliance on the unsourced migration narrative; that narrative’s precise Scottish birth and travel details remain unverified.

Glasgow-1552.role: The original 1825 will explicitly names William among John’s children and gives him a $200 legacy. The existing William account is the compatible circa-1781 son already represented in this family. This is direct evidence for the family relationship, while the at-sea birth and exact later adult dates remain inherited claims rather than facts established by the will.

Glasgow-1553.role: The original 1825 will explicitly names Matthew among John’s children and gives him a $200 legacy. The existing Matthew account has the same family placement and a compatible circa-1787 Antis generation. The father identification is now supported by an original parent statement rather than a census slot or contributed child list; the will does not verify Matthew’s exact birth or later death.

Glasgow-36.role: The original will names Taylor as John’s son, gives him a wagon and a joint share of the Antis home tract with James, and appoints James and Taylor executors. The existing Taylor Wilson account’s Antis household and reproduced 1889 obituary describing his removal with his father to a local farm in 1810 strongly identify this son. The obituary is a held transcription, not a newly inspected newspaper image. Conflicting inherited birth and death dates remain unchanged.

Glasgow-664.role: The original will now proves that the Antis/Sinking Valley John had a son John. This independently supports the previously compiled report of a young emigrant son John. The Cambria adult’s reported 1777 Scottish generation, 1820 Allegheny Township household and central Pennsylvania continuity make him the leading checked identity for that son. The will supplies no residence, wife or age for its John, so identification with the Cambria adult remains a probable inference. Daill and Glasgow birthplace claims are not equated or verified.

Glasgow-1984.role: The original will explicitly names a son Samuel and gives him a $50 legacy. Samuel Glasgow-1984’s reported circa-1786 Antis birth and 1829 Huntingdon death fit the testator’s Antis household and father generation. The previously suggested John family is now supported by an actual named-son clause and a specific locality match. The bounded catalogue comparison found no stronger same-generation Antis Samuel. The will gives no Samuel residence, age or spouse, and his profile dates remain derivative, so the complete identity and father proposition is probable at 88%, not certain. Samuel’s reported death before the legacy’s 1832 due date is not a contradiction: the will provides for a deceased child’s issue.

Glasgow-2577.role: The original will names James as a son, joint devisee of the Antis home tract and executor with Taylor. James Glasgow-2577 is the strongest checked adult match: reported born in Blair County on 4 October 1793, with a daughter Mary Ellen reported born there in 1829 and eventual Logan Valley Cemetery burial. His age about31 at probate fits. These profile and daughter details are derivative and their memorial originals were not inspected. The bounded public-catalogue comparison found no closer local same-generation James. The Missouri James-45 remains a compatible alternative by name, generation and broad Pennsylvania origin, but his probable Downington birth and later Missouri household are a weaker locality match. The will supplies no age, wife or residence for its James; select2577 as an80% probable working father connection, retaining the alternative and all vital fields.

Glasgow-45.role: Compatible unselected James candidate; executor identity unresolved

The widow Margaret is not automatically each child’s mother. Richard’s father confidence rises 72%→97%, William’s 65%→96%, Matthew’s 64%→96%, Taylor’s 64%→98%, and the Cambria John’s 57%→86%. Earlier statements that the will was uninspected, or that Samuel had only a census-age slot, are superseded by this original reading.

Glasglow-11.role: Jane Dysart’s named child group; mother’s father not stated

note: Alexander’s independently documented children James, Mary and Ann match the 1892 citation’s Alexander-of-Rasharkin group. That group appears among heirs/next of kin before the separate legatee list. Nancy’s own niece/nephew statements, linked through the Dysart and Anderson baptisms, anchor the family interpretation. John-867’s distinctive James Garvin/Ann branch identifies the other cited household, and his 1846 marriage names father John Glasgow, farmer. Recorded Glasgow birth surnames favor a common paternal family. The combined identity and kinship argument supports a confident 90% inference; a generic unsupported half-sibling possibility does not impose a probable ceiling. The probate citation is an incomplete service notice, not an adjudicated pedigree: Alexander’s living son Robert was omitted. John’s Ballydonnelly description and the cited Lizzie remain unexplained. The underlying petition and heir schedule have not been inspected. These are real limits, but no held competing household matches the James Garvin/Ann group and no evidence identifies different Glasgow fathers through a maternal half-sibling relationship. The flax-grower and older Larne identities remain separate hypotheses.

note: The visually checked 1903 family memorial, PDF p.17, explicitly names William Glasgow of Killycorragh and Nancy Glendinning as parents of five sons, Henry Cunningham, Adam, Isaac Watts, Benjamin and Alexander Flemming, and three daughters, Mary, Matilda and Jane. Nancy’s reported April 1803 birth and 20 March 1890 Belle Center death anchor this particular family. This is a retrospective family publication, not an original baptism register. Earlier WikiTree Space citations derive from the same publication and are not independent witnesses. The list gives no dates or spouses for the children and does not establish an interleaved birth order. Each percentage concerns the specific father-profile pair, with later adult identity assessed separately. William’s own father remains unknown and unrated; Adam-3151 remains 77% probable because the 1834/1840 birth claims and Arthur’s Ohio-born son Adam-2387 are unresolved. Henry Cunningham-3148 and Isaac Watts-3149 remain 92%. No maternal assessment, structured vital field, selected father ID or live WikiTree flag is changed.

historical_basis.reason: The historical paragraph lists the eight children before their mother’s explicitly dated20March1890death. This is a conservative privacy bound, not a new individual birth estimate; retained profile birth dates are1824–1844.

The head’s wife Margaret, 1846 marriage year, residence, parish and farming occupation uniquely fit John’s father-naming 1846 marriage. On the ordinary meaning of the documented brotherhood and the shared Glasgow surname, John’s named father John Glasgow, farmer, is confidently Samuel’s father at 95%. note: The original 1851 Glenleslie household 21 return records John Glasgow as 100, Rose as 80, and 1791 for both. Its marriage heading asks “In what Year Married, or in what Years if more than once?” The detailed transcription’s first-marriage field is therefore an editorial description, not the literal question on this return. Only 1791 is entered: an earlier union is not documented, and the request for multiple years means its absence still weighs against a straightforward earlier-marriage explanation. The original also calls the forty-year-old John a nephew and gives his occupation as vagrant; the 1839 marriage belongs to him. The mortality table explicitly calls Andrew Glasgow, a thirty-year-old linen weaver who died of consumption in winter 1848, a son of the head. It does not name Andrew’s mother. 38% assesses the complete John-to-Robert profile hypothesis, not the certainty of reading the census. Robert’s census-implied birth about 1778–1779 precedes the sole reported marriage year by roughly twelve years. An earlier union, nonmarital fatherhood or a reporting error would still be needed, and none is established. The original asks for multiple marriage years, so omission of an earlier year remains a real limitation. John’s exceptional age may be inaccurate. An uncle, cousin, other collateral relative or unrepresented father remains possible; the older Alexander comparison is not excluded. Rose’s reported age does not fit her as Robert’s mother, and no mother or earlier wife is assigned. The selection concerns the 1851 Glenleslie man only: it does not identify him with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier, validate every attached child, or prove a Y-DNA pedigree. Hugh-3956’s 74% brother hypothesis includes a separate identity uncertainty and is not automatically assigned this father; his estimated earlier generation also needs its own chronology test. The inherited Unknown Glasgow-3905 is preserved as an uncertain alternative with no invented percentage. No live WikiTree family field is changed.

assessment:
**Original will, 23 October 2026:** Samuel Glasgow of West Fallowfield names wife **Tabitha**, infant daughter **Margaret Ellen**, and a contingent remainder to the **sons of his three brothers William, James and Robert Glasgow, of Ireland**. The three named men are the testator’s brothers; the beneficiaries are their sons. This is not a clause naming the testator’s own son James. The will is dated **17 May 1824**; the proving endorsement is **31 May 1824**. [County original](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=773006&page=588&repo=r-24f48cc6), file 7520, scanned volume 07451–7600, portal pp. 588–589 (downloaded extract pp. 3–4). Cover is portal p. 586. Original pages were visually read; the brother clause was independently reread.

The will appoints Robert Futhey and Thomas Stewart executors; estate office does not establish kinship. It also names Samuel Glasgow Haslett, described as James Haslett’s infant twin son; no godparent relationship is stated. His Glasgow middle name does not make him a Glasgow son. Later accounts, portal pp. 594 and 596, name Benjamin Glasgow as a debtor and William Glasgow in transmitting another estate’s legacy, without stating their relationship to the testator.

**Profile identity:** [Samuel Glasgow-2872](/people/glasgow-2872.html) remains a compatible candidate, not an established identification. His retained Cochranville locality and exact 17 May 1824 date fit this estate closely, but that date is the will date and may have been inherited as a death date. The will alone cannot prove death on that day. The profile’s Judith, who died in 1812, does not exclude a later Tabitha marriage. Its Pennsylvania birth/parent reconstruction and the brothers in Ireland need a combined family test rather than an automatic rejection or merge. No other local Tabitha or Margaret Ellen catalogue identity was found in the bounded duplicate check. The existing 72% father assessment and all family/vital fields are retained; this source does not name the testator’s father.

**Missouri comparison:** [James Glasgow-45](/people/glasgow-45.html), the probable Downington-born drummer, is not named in the inspected will or later accounts. That absence does not establish that he was not a son, but neither the military entry nor this estate selects a named father. The new Ireland relatives supply a concrete family to investigate while the immigrant-father/Philadelphia-estate tradition remains unproved. The complete downloaded estate extract is retained privately; no manuscript image is republished.
note: Samuel-1492 is reviewed as the letter-defined emigrant son. The independently inspected 1824 West Fallowfield will names brothers William, James and Robert of Ireland, a distinctive match to that sibling set. This supports the family reconstruction while the testator’s profile identity remains open. Those names must not be attributed to this page. It is an original scan of a late 1886 compilation, not an original eighteenth-century birth or death entry. Its informant and independence from later family tradition are unknown.

The reviewed Chester tax index lists John with 80 acres in West Nottingham in 1787–1791 and Hugh with 80 acres in 1793–1799, after John’s recorded 1792 death. That consecutive name, locality and acreage pattern supports family succession, but the tax index is not a conveyance proving the same parcel or a father–son relationship. The newly inspected Gibson p. 414 names neither parent and instead says Hugh’s father emigrated about 1730 and died in 1772. Those dates conflict with John-2871’s retained 1738 birth and 1792 death. The late history may contain errors, so the existing father remains probable, but its general Nottingham context cannot be counted as independent agreement on this particular John. File 4225 independently documents a John’s 1792 East Nottingham estate; it does not name Hugh in the inspected surviving papers.

The index succession remains useful circumstantial evidence; the unnamed 1886 paternal account is substantive counterevidence. Neither John-2870 nor the 1789 shoemaker is selected as a replacement. No parent is detached, and no vital field or mother is changed.

The 1730/1772 account does not identify John-2870 either: child migration in 1730 would fit his 1722 baptism, but the retained May 1769 death conflicts with 1772. A September 1769 Hugh birth after a May death would permit posthumous fatherhood and is not an exclusion. No replacement father or mother follows.

Glasgow the congressman Hugh Glasgow’s son and locates his farm about a mile south of the old Glasgow homestead, on the Maryland side of the Mason–Dixon line. The existing Cunningham Ramsay-3742, born 1806, is the adult son of that distinctive name in Hugh’s family. The other Cunningham, Sample-3747, died in infancy and cannot be the mature farmer described. 97% is a confident identification of the existing father–child profile pair from an explicit son statement in a late compiled history. It is not a newly discovered birth entry. assessment:
**Two original estates, not one John:** [file 4015](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772934&page=1065&repo=r-24f48cc6), West Nottingham, contains an administration bond dated 31 March 1789, an inventory dated 26 March, and Peter Glasgow’s signed certificate of 26 March. Peter says the deceased John lived at his house about 27 years, was his uncle, and died intestate. Peter asks that John Taylor, **Peter’s sister’s son**, administer. The bond appoints John Taylor; William Edmonston and Henry McCormick are securities, not kin established by their office. The inventory includes eleven old shoemaker lasts. The next estate begins at portal p. 1067. [Complete connected family drafts and candidate review](/research/subjects/nottingham-probate/#john-shoemaker).

[File 4225](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772936&page=247&repo=r-24f48cc6), East Nottingham, has an inventory dated **31 May 1792**, followed by its June oath. Portal p. 249 includes a debt against the estate of **John Glasgow, shoemaker, deceased**. The distinctive occupation, earlier death and nearby place make the 1789 uncle a probable identification of this deceased debtor; the debt does not prove the two Johns were related. The file’s replacement slip says the original administration bond is missing and directs the reader to **Administration Book 2, p. 386**. The next estate begins at portal p. 251. The surviving file does not supply a named Hugh heir.

John-2871, whose death is recorded in 1792, is a compatible candidate for the 1792 estate, with an East/West Nottingham locality question still open. The 1789 uncle cannot be assigned to John-2870 (retained death 1769) or John-2871 (1792) without resolving those actual conflicts. No generic name match, estate office or debt is converted into a father relationship. The inventory and bond dates are not exact death dates.
